title: JESUS CALLED IT ADULTERY… EVEN WHEN NOBODY TOUCHED ANYBODY.
paragraphs: JESUS CALLED IT ADULTERY… EVEN WHEN NOBODY TOUCHED ANYBODY.
Why One Sentence From Jesus Exposes the Secret Battles Behind Our Screens, the Desires We Keep Feeding, and the Hearts We Keep Hiding — Matthew 5:27–28
Nobody saw you.
Nobody heard anything.
There was no hotel room. No secret meeting. No physical affair. No evidence that anyone could hold against you.
Just a glance.
A thought.
A moment you could have walked away from… but didn't.
And perhaps the most frightening part wasn't what you saw.
It was how long you wanted to keep looking.
Then Jesus spoke words that shattered humanity's comfortable definition of faithfulness.
“But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.” — Matthew 5:28, KJV
Already.
That is the word that should make us stop.
Not eventually. Not if you act on it. Not when somebody discovers what you have been doing.
Already.

But before you misunderstand Jesus and begin drowning in guilt over every unwanted thought, every moment of attraction, or every temptation you never invited, you need to understand what He actually said.
Because Jesus was not teaching that noticing beauty is adultery.
He was exposing something far more deliberate.
And what He revealed on that mountainside still reaches into bedrooms, marriages, private messages, social media feeds, and the hidden places of our hearts nearly two thousand years later.
The question is not simply whether your hands have remained innocent.
The question is whether your heart has been quietly practicing a betrayal your hands have not yet committed.
And if that question makes you uncomfortable, don't leave yet.
Because the same Jesus who exposes the heart is the Savior who can make it new.
Imagine standing among the crowd listening to Jesus deliver the Sermon on the Mount.
Some listeners had spent their lives trying to obey the commandments. They knew the law. They knew the boundaries. They knew that adultery was forbidden.
Jesus began with something familiar.
“Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery.” — Matthew 5:27, KJV
The commandment came from Exodus 20:14 and Deuteronomy 5:18.
In Hebrew, Exodus 20:14 reads:
לֹא תִּנְאָף
Lo tin'af.
“You shall not commit adultery.”
The commandment protected the sacred covenant of marriage against sexual unfaithfulness.
But Jesus did something astonishing.
He did not weaken the commandment.
He revealed its deeper moral reach.
The people listening could no longer measure faithfulness merely by what they had physically done.
Jesus directed their attention to what they were deliberately cultivating inside.
The Greek text of Matthew 5:28 says:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.
A close rendering is:
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Look carefully at one expression.
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
Pros to epithymēsai autēn.
This construction points toward looking with the purpose of desiring her.
The verb epithymeō means to desire, long for, or covet. It is not inherently sinful in every biblical context. Its moral significance depends on what is desired and how.
In this passage, the context is sexual desire directed toward someone in a way that violates the faithfulness and purity Jesus commands.
That distinction matters.
Jesus is not condemning the involuntary recognition that someone is attractive.
He is confronting the intentional gaze that welcomes, cultivates, and indulges forbidden sexual desire.
There is a difference between seeing someone and choosing to turn that person into an object of sexual gratification in your imagination.
There is a difference between temptation arriving and deliberately entertaining it.
There is a difference between an unwanted thought crossing your mind and willingly making a home for it.
Temptation may knock without your permission. But you are responsible for how you respond when it knocks.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that Jesus was tempted, yet without sin.
Therefore, temptation itself cannot automatically be identical to sin.
This matters especially for the believer who has been tormented by intrusive thoughts, unwanted images, or fears that a passing temptation has already destroyed their relationship with God.
Jesus does not call you guilty simply because something unwanted entered your awareness.
He calls you to resist sin rather than nourish it.
But there is another side to this truth.
Some of us have become remarkably skilled at calling deliberate indulgence an accident.
We say, “I was just scrolling.”
But we returned to the same profile.
We say, “I didn't mean anything by it.”
But we kept searching for more.
We say, “Nothing happened.”
But in our imagination, we allowed things we would never admit aloud.
We say, “It's harmless.”
But we are increasingly dissatisfied with the person we promised to love.
And sometimes, the most dangerous lie is not that God cannot see us.
It is that what God sees does not matter.
Consider the husband sitting beside his wife while she sleeps.
She believes they are sharing a quiet evening.
His phone illuminates his face.
One image becomes another.
One video becomes another.
He knows he should stop.
He tells himself he will stop after the next one.
Then the next.
Then another.
Eventually, he puts the phone away.
Nothing physical happened with another person.
No conversation took place.
No meeting was arranged.
But something has been happening in the privacy of his desires.
The woman sleeping beside him has no idea that his attention has been repeatedly surrendered elsewhere.
Now imagine the wife who has begun nurturing an intimate fantasy about a man outside her marriage.
Perhaps he listens carefully. Perhaps he compliments her. Perhaps he makes her feel noticed in ways she has not felt for years.
She tells herself that nothing is wrong because there has been no physical contact.
But she keeps imagining a different life.
A different embrace.
A different relationship.
A version of herself that belongs to someone else.
The circumstances are different, but the spiritual question remains.
What are we allowing our hearts to desire, and what are we doing to cultivate that desire?
Jesus was not speaking only to married men.
His words confront the sexual integrity of every disciple.
The unmarried believer who secretly indulges in fantasies that disregard another person's dignity.
The married believer who treats a spouse's trust as something that only physical contact can violate.
The person who repeatedly consumes pornography while insisting that nobody is being hurt.
The Christian who maintains a respectable public image while privately surrendering to habits they know are pulling them away from obedience.
And the person who is already ashamed, already fighting, already wondering whether freedom is even possible.
Jesus sees the whole person.
Not merely the public behavior.
Not merely the reputation.
Not merely the carefully edited version of ourselves that appears on Sunday morning.
The heart.
In biblical language, the heart is not simply the place where emotions happen. It is the inner center of our desires, intentions, thoughts, and moral decisions.
That is why Proverbs 4:23 says:
“Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.”
What we repeatedly welcome into our inner lives shapes how we think, what we desire, and eventually how we act.
And this is where Jesus' teaching becomes painfully personal.
Because many people are asking the wrong question.
“How far can I go without technically committing adultery?”
Jesus redirects us toward a better question.
“How can I become faithful in the deepest places of my heart?”
There is a world of difference between those questions.
One searches for a loophole.
The other seeks holiness.
One asks how much darkness can remain without consequences.
The other asks how much of the heart can be surrendered to Christ.
And here is something our generation desperately needs to hear.
A person can remain physically faithful while deliberately nurturing desires that contradict the faithfulness Jesus commands.
But this does not mean every sin of the heart is identical in its earthly consequences to a physical affair.
Jesus' statement establishes the seriousness of inward sin; it does not erase meaningful distinctions between thoughts and actions.
A physical affair can involve additional betrayal, deception, exploitation, broken trust, and devastating consequences.
Jesus does not minimize those realities.
He refuses to let the absence of physical action become an excuse for cherished inward unfaithfulness.
And perhaps that is why His words are so unsettling.
They remove our ability to hide behind technical innocence.
We may be able to say, “I never touched anyone.”
But can we truthfully say, “I have guarded what I willingly allowed my heart to pursue”?
That question is not meant to destroy you.
It is meant to awaken you.
Because sin often begins long before anyone else can recognize its consequences.
James 1:14–15 describes the progression of desire when it draws a person toward sin, and how sin, when fully grown, brings forth death.
The warning is not that every desire inevitably becomes an outward act.
It is that indulged sinful desire is spiritually dangerous.
What we continually feed becomes harder to resist.
What we repeatedly excuse becomes easier to justify.
And what we refuse to confront can gradually shape the person we are becoming.
This is why Job made a remarkable declaration.
“I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?” — Job 31:1, KJV
Job understood that faithfulness involved the eyes as well as the body.
He recognized the relationship between what he chose to look at and what he allowed himself to desire.
Centuries later, Jesus brought that same seriousness into His teaching.
And then, in Matthew 5:29–30, He used startling imagery about removing an eye or cutting off a hand if it causes sin.
These are deliberately forceful illustrations of the seriousness of sin, not instructions to injure yourself.
Jesus was calling His followers to deal decisively with whatever leads them into sin.
For some people today, that might mean deleting an application.
For others, ending a secret conversation.
For someone else, installing content restrictions, seeking accountability, or admitting to a trusted Christian mentor that a private habit has become difficult to control.
For a married couple, it may mean confronting dishonesty and rebuilding trust through repentance, patience, and genuine change.
For someone whose compulsive sexual behavior has become deeply entrenched, it may also mean seeking help from a qualified mental health professional alongside wise spiritual support.
None of those actions purchases God's forgiveness.
They are practical responses to the call to turn away from sin.
And no, you do not have to pretend that the struggle is easy.
Sometimes obedience looks like closing the screen while your body is still urging you to continue.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to reopen a conversation you know is becoming inappropriate.
Sometimes it looks like telling the truth when every instinct tells you to hide.
Sometimes it looks like getting up after another failure, confessing honestly, and refusing to make peace with what is destroying your spiritual life.
There may be tears.
There may be difficult conversations.
There may be consequences that cannot be instantly repaired.
But repentance is not merely feeling terrible about what happened.
It is turning toward God with a willingness to leave the sin behind.
And now we arrive at the part of this passage that must never be forgotten.
Jesus did not expose the heart because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
He came to save sinners.
The same Christ who said that lustful looking could constitute adultery in the heart also gave His life for people whose hearts were corrupted by sin.
That includes sexual sin.
That includes hidden sin.
That includes sins committed while nobody was watching.
And it includes the person reading this who has begun to believe that forgiveness is available for everyone except them.
Listen carefully.
Your sin is serious.
But Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
You do not need a softer definition of sin.
You need the grace of the One who died and rose again to rescue sinners from its guilt and power.
The cross does not tell us that sin was insignificant.
The cross tells us that God's mercy is greater than our ability to save ourselves.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had finally cleaned up every secret habit.
Not after we had established an impressive record of moral perfection.
Not after we had convinced ourselves that we were worthy of being loved.
Christ died for sinners.
And because Jesus rose from the dead, the Gospel offers more than a temporary emotional release from guilt.
It announces forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and the promise of a transformed life through Christ.
First John 1:9 gives this assurance:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice the word cleanse.
God does not merely invite you to cover the stain.
He invites you to bring your sin into the light.
Not so you can earn His love through public humiliation.
Not so strangers can demand the details of your private failures.
But so that you can stop defending what needs to be surrendered.
There is a kind of exhaustion that comes from maintaining two versions of yourself.
The person everyone knows.
And the person you are terrified they might discover.
You laugh with your friends.
You worship with the congregation.
You post Bible verses.
You encourage others.
And then, when you are alone, you return to the very behavior you keep promising God you will abandon.
Afterward, the familiar shame returns.
You feel disgusted with yourself.
You wonder whether your prayers are still being heard.
You promise that this time will be different.
Then another temptation comes.
And the cycle begins again.
If that describes you, please understand something important.
Shame alone cannot produce the transformation that only God's grace can sustain.
Second Corinthians 7:10 distinguishes godly sorrow that leads to repentance from worldly sorrow that produces death.
There is a difference between conviction that draws you back to Christ and despair that tells you to run away from Him.
Conviction says, “This sin must be brought into the light.”
Despair says, “You are beyond redemption.”
Conviction calls you to repentance.
Despair tempts you to surrender hope.
And the Gospel gives us a reason to reject despair.
Romans 8:1 says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
That is not permission to continue deliberately in sin.
Romans 6:1–2 explicitly rejects the idea that grace gives believers permission to remain in sin.
It is the assurance that those who belong to Christ are not left to face condemnation for sins He has borne.
His grace both forgives and teaches us to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 describes God's grace as training us to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Real grace does not whisper, “Keep doing whatever you want.”
Real grace calls us away from what enslaves us and toward the Savior who makes us new.
Perhaps you have failed more times than you can count.
Perhaps you are married and know you have wounded the trust of someone who loves you.
Perhaps you are single and have spent years believing that purity is impossible in a world saturated with sexual temptation.
Perhaps you have never told another human being what you have been struggling with.
Or perhaps you have been harmed by someone else's sexual betrayal, and this teaching brings back memories you never wanted to revisit.
If you are the person who was betrayed, hear this too.
Jesus' words do not make you responsible for another person's choices.
You are not required to pretend the betrayal was harmless.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust, remove consequences, or require you to remain in an unsafe relationship.
Truth, accountability, and protection matter.
And if you are the one who sinned, repentance does not mean demanding immediate forgiveness or restored trust from someone you have hurt.
It means taking responsibility, telling the truth, accepting appropriate consequences, and allowing genuine change to be demonstrated over time.
Jesus cares about both holiness and the people wounded when holiness is abandoned.
That is why His teaching must never be twisted into a weapon for shaming victims or excusing offenders.
And there is another truth we must recover.
The people we look at are not objects created to satisfy our desires.
They are human beings made in the image of God.
They have names.
Families.
Histories.
Wounds.
Hopes.
Dignity.
When Jesus calls us away from lust, He is not calling us to despise human beauty or fear other people.
He is calling us to love others without reducing them to instruments of our gratification.
To see a person rather than merely a body.
To honor marriage rather than secretly undermine it.
To practice self-control rather than surrender every impulse to the authority of appetite.
To recognize that another person's humanity matters even when no one else knows what we are thinking.
And that kind of transformation reaches much deeper than a rule about where to direct your eyes.
It reaches into the question of who governs your heart.
Because the ultimate goal of Christian purity is not simply to avoid scandal.
It is to become more like Jesus.
Not merely respectable in public.
But increasingly faithful in private.
Not merely afraid of getting caught.
But sincerely desiring what honors God.
Not merely resisting consequences.
But learning to love righteousness.
That is the difference between managing an image and surrendering a life.
And it is why the Gospel Warrior message remains so urgent:
Not because every scandal disappears.
Not because every consequence is erased.
Not because broken trust automatically returns.
But because sin does not have to be the final chapter of a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
A person who once lived in deception can learn to walk in truth.
A person who repeatedly surrendered to lust can grow in self-control.
A marriage wounded by betrayal may, where safety, genuine repentance, and mutual willingness exist, begin the difficult work of healing.
A believer trapped in shame can discover that confession is not the end of their story.
And someone who has never trusted Christ can hear the invitation to repent, believe the Gospel, and receive new life in Him.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That promise does not mean every temptation instantly disappears.
It means that belonging to Christ changes the foundation and direction of your life.
You are no longer called to make peace with the sin that once ruled you.
You are called to follow the Savior who redeemed you.
So perhaps the most important question today is not whether you have ever looked with lust.
Perhaps the more important question is what you will do now that Jesus has shown you the seriousness of the heart.
Will you defend the habit?
Will you minimize it?
Will you hide behind the argument that nobody was physically hurt?
Will you keep promising to change while refusing to remove what continually draws you back?
Or will you finally come to Jesus without pretending?
You do not have to tell the entire internet the details of your private struggle.
But you can be honest before God.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can seek appropriate help.
You can begin replacing secrecy with accountability and deliberate obedience.
You can ask the Holy Spirit to renew your desires.
You can choose today not to feed what you are asking God to help you overcome.
And when the battle returns tomorrow, you can return again to the means of grace God has provided: prayer, Scripture, fellowship, wise counsel, and dependence on Christ.
Not to purchase salvation.
But because the Savior who saves us also calls us to follow Him.
You do not owe anyone a public confession of intimate details. A simple request for prayer is enough.
Your words may encourage another believer who is struggling to believe that change is possible.
Somebody reading those comments may have been fighting alone for years.
Let them know that the church should be a place where truth is spoken, repentance is encouraged, and wounded people are treated with compassion.
And please, do not let this message end with you.
Not to expose someone.
Not to embarrass a spouse.
Not to make a public accusation against a person you suspect is struggling.
It is about surrendering the heart.
There is another way you can help this mission reach people who may never walk into a church or ask anyone for spiritual help.
Think about the person who reads a Gospel-centered message at two in the morning while battling temptation.
The believer who is too ashamed to ask a question in church.
The husband or wife who needs to hear that repentance involves more than saying sorry.
The young Christian trying to understand what Scripture actually teaches.
The exhausted soul who needs to be reminded that Christ still receives repentant sinners.
And if you are already committed to giving faithfully to your local church, please do not misunderstand this invitation.
Scripture encourages generous, willing giving, not giving driven by guilt or pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
You do not need to pay a ministry to receive God's forgiveness.
And you do not need to purchase access to the grace that Jesus Christ freely gives.
These products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, thoughtful gifts, and resources for Christian encouragement.
The library is part of our desire to make Christian learning and spiritual nourishment accessible.
Some people can give financially.
Others can share, pray, encourage, and invite.
Every act of sincere support should come from love for Christ and His Gospel, never from fear that God will love you less if you cannot contribute.
Because the greatest goal is not to build an audience that merely admires Christian content.
It is to help people encounter the truth of Scripture, follow Jesus Christ, and grow as His disciples.
And now, before you close this article, return with me to the words that started everything.
“Hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
Already.
Jesus knew that the heart could cross a moral boundary before the body ever moved.
But He also knew something else.
He knew that human hearts needed more than warnings.
They needed redemption.
That is why the Sermon on the Mount cannot be separated from the cross.
The One who taught the holiness of God would ultimately bear the sins of His people.
The One who exposed hidden guilt would give His life to provide forgiveness.
The One who called for purity would pour out His Spirit to transform those who belong to Him.
Jesus does not merely tell sinners to try harder and leave them to save themselves.
He calls us to repent, believe, abide in Him, and walk in the new life that His grace makes possible.
So tonight, when the screen lights up…
When the temptation returns…
When the familiar thought tries to persuade you that nobody will know…
Remember that the question is not simply whether someone can see you.
Remember the Savior who sees you completely and still calls you to come to Him.
You can close the screen.
You can end the conversation.
You can confess the sin.
You can ask for help.
You can choose obedience.
And when you fail, you can refuse both excuses and despair, returning to Christ in genuine repentance.
Because the Christian life is not a performance of flawless self-sufficiency.
It is a life of faith, repentance, obedience, and dependence upon the Savior.
The heart that once welcomed darkness can learn to love the light.
The eyes that once searched for opportunities to lust can learn to look at others with dignity.
The person who once defended secret sin can learn to confess it.
And the soul that once believed its story was over can discover that Jesus Christ still calls sinners into new life.
Not as a performance.
Not as a promise that you will never struggle again.
But as a prayer that the hidden places of your life would increasingly belong to Him.
Because there may be someone silently wondering whether the worst thing they have done in secret has permanently disqualified them from the love of God.
Let them hear the Gospel.
Let them hear the call to repentance.
Let them hear that forgiveness is found in Jesus Christ.
Let them hear that holiness is not merely about what the world can see.
And let them hear that no sinner is saved by hiding successfully.
The most dangerous secret is not the sin you are afraid someone will discover, but the sin you have stopped bringing to the Savior who can forgive and transform you.
